samf-junior-2011-r2-01.title: Rewrite the fractions
samf-junior-2011-r2-01.body:
Each fraction has the form $\frac{n+10}{n}=1+\frac{10}{n}$ with $n=19,29,39,49,59$. All lie between $1$ and $2$, so the closest to $2$ is the largest, which has the smallest $n$: $\frac{29}{19}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac{29}{19}$**

samf-junior-2011-r2-02.title: Sum of divisors
samf-junior-2011-r2-02.body:
The factors of $40$ are $1,2,4,5,8,10,20,40$ with sum $90$. Since he got $70$, he left out $90-70=20$.

**Answer: (E) 20**

samf-junior-2011-r2-03.title: Count per block
samf-junior-2011-r2-03.body:
A structure of length $1$ is a box with $12$ rods. Each extra unit of length adds a new box sharing one face (4 rods) with the previous one, so it needs $12-4=8$ more rods. Length $n$ needs $12+8(n-1)=8n+4$ rods; for $n=40$: $324$. (Check: length $2$ gives $20$ rods.)

**Answer: (A) 324**

samf-junior-2011-r2-04.title: Split the power
samf-junior-2011-r2-04.body:
$20^{11}=2^{11}\cdot10^{11}=2048\cdot10^{11}=2.048\times10^{14}$. The number $2048$ has $4$ digits, followed by $11$ zeros: $15$ digits.

**Answer: (E) 15**

samf-junior-2011-r2-05.title: Multiply the remaining fractions
samf-junior-2011-r2-05.body:
After the first gift she has $90\%$; after the second she keeps $80\%$ of that: $0.9\times0.8=0.72=72\%$.

**Answer: (B) 72**

samf-junior-2011-r2-07.title: Time then distance
samf-junior-2011-r2-07.body:
Boris needs $\frac4{10}=0.4$ h. In that time Otto travels $6\cdot0.4=2.4$ km further away, so he is $8+2.4=10.4$ km from $O$.

**Answer: (D) 10,4 km**

samf-junior-2011-r2-08.title: Whole tiles and cut tiles
samf-junior-2011-r2-08.body:
Put the right angle at the origin, legs $6$ (horizontal) and $3$ (vertical); the hypotenuse passes through the lattice points $(0,3),(2,2),(4,1),(6,0)$. Tiles lying completely inside the triangle: $4$ in the bottom row and $2$ in the middle row, so $6$ whole tiles. The remaining area $9-6=3$ consists of three right triangles with legs $2$ and $1$ along the hypotenuse, each of area $1$. Each such triangle spans two columns: it is a trapezoid piece in one tile together with a small triangle (legs $1$ and $\frac12$) in the next. Cutting one tile gives the trapezoid and a small triangle congruent to the piece needed in the neighbouring column, so one cut tile supplies a whole triangle of area $1$. Hence $3$ cut tiles are needed, and at least $6+3=9$ tiles in all.

**Answer: (C) 9**

samf-junior-2011-r2-10.title: Use triangle APB
samf-junior-2011-r2-10.body:
Triangle $APB$ has base $AB$ (a side of the rectangle) and apex $P$ on the opposite side, so it is half the rectangle. Hence $\triangle ADP+\triangle PBC=\frac12$ of the rectangle, and the shaded triangle $PBC$ is $\frac12-\frac15=\frac3{10}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac3{10}$**

samf-junior-2011-r2-11.title: Search the sequence
samf-junior-2011-r2-11.body:
The numbers come from $6,13,20,27,34,41,48,55,\dots$. If $6$ is used, the others must be odd and not multiples of $3$: $13,41,55,\dots$, giving at least $6+13+41+55=115$. Without $6$: $20$ and $34$ share a factor $2$, so among $13,20,27,34,41$ we can use at most one of them: the best is $13,20,27,41$ with sum $101$ (all pairs coprime: $20=2^2\cdot5$, $27=3^3$, $13$ and $41$ prime). Any other choice (e.g. $13,27,34,41$ or using $48$ or more) gives a larger sum.

**Answer: (B) 101**

samf-junior-2011-r2-12.title: Weeks and leftover days
samf-junior-2011-r2-12.body:
$366=52\cdot7+2$, so every weekday occurs $52$ times and exactly two weekdays (those of the first two days of the year) occur $53$ times. Sunday is one of them with probability $\frac27$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac27$**

samf-junior-2011-r2-13.title: Maximise the hidden odds
samf-junior-2011-r2-13.body:
The two cards showing an even number must have an odd number on the back: $2$ odd numbers. The four cards showing an odd number can have anything on the back, so up to $4$ more odd numbers. The total is $4$ (visible) $+2+4=10$.

**Answer: (D) 10**

samf-junior-2011-r2-14.title: Original side and perimeter
samf-junior-2011-r2-14.body:
The removed area is $1+4+9+36=50$ cm$^2$, which is half the original, so the original square has area $100$ and side $10$ cm. Cutting a square from a corner replaces two edges by two edges of the same total length, so the perimeter does not change: $4\cdot10=40$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 40 cm**

samf-junior-2011-r2-15.title: Equation
samf-junior-2011-r2-15.body:
Let there be $2a$ boys and $3a$ girls. Then $\frac{2a+5}{3a}=\frac7{10}$, so $20a+50=21a$, $a=50$, and there are $3a=150$ girls.

**Answer: (E) 150**

samf-junior-2011-r2-16.title: Equilateral triangle
samf-junior-2011-r2-16.body:
Let the centres be $O_1,O_2$. Then $O_1O_2=2$ and $O_1A=O_2A=2$, so $\triangle O_1O_2A$ is equilateral with side $2$. The line $AB$ is perpendicular to $O_1O_2$ and bisects it, so half of $AB$ is the height of this triangle, $\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3$. Hence $AB=2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: (D) $2\sqrt3$**

samf-junior-2011-r2-17.title: Overlap of semicircles and square
samf-junior-2011-r2-17.body:
The four semicircles (radius $1$, drawn inwards) together have area $4\cdot\frac12\pi=2\pi$. They cover the whole square (area $4$) and the leaves are exactly the places where they overlap, so the leaf area is $2\pi-4$.

**Answer: (B) $2\pi-4$**

samf-junior-2011-r2-17.title: One leaf at a time
samf-junior-2011-r2-17.body:
Take the semicircles on two adjacent sides, centred at the midpoints $M_1$, $M_2$. Both circles pass through the centre $O$ of the square and the common corner $C$, and $\angle OM_1C=90^\circ$. The overlap is two congruent circular segments, each a quarter circle of radius $1$ ($\frac\pi4$) minus a right triangle with legs $1$ ($\frac12$). One leaf is $2\left(\frac\pi4-\frac12\right)=\frac\pi2-1$, and four leaves give $2\pi-4$.

**Answer: (B) $2\pi-4$**

samf-junior-2011-r2-18.title: Divisible by 99
samf-junior-2011-r2-18.body:
If the digits are $X,Y,Z$ then $(100X+10Y+Z)-(100Z+10Y+X)=99(X-Z)$. So the result is a multiple of $99$. Among the options only $198=2\cdot99$ is one ($729,189,459,759$ are not).

**Answer: (C) 198**

samf-junior-2011-r2-19.title: Name the lengths
samf-junior-2011-r2-19.body:
Let the original rectangle be $W\times H$ with $H<W$. Removing a square of side $H$ leaves an $H\times s$ rectangle with $s=W-H$; removing a square of side $s$ leaves the final rectangle $s\times t$ with $t=H-s$. So $H=s+t$ and $W=H+s=2s+t$. The perimeter condition $2(s+t)=\frac38\cdot2(W+H)=\frac38\cdot2(3s+2t)$ gives $8(s+t)=3(3s+2t)$, i.e. $s=2t$. Then $H:W=(s+t):(2s+t)=3t:5t=3:5$.

**Answer: (A) 3 : 5**

samf-junior-2011-r2-19.title: Check
samf-junior-2011-r2-19.body:
Take $H=3$, $W=5$: remove a $3\times3$ square, leaving $3\times2$; remove a $2\times2$ square, leaving $2\times1$ with perimeter $6$. The original perimeter is $16$ and $\frac38\cdot16=6$. ✓

**Answer: (A) 3 : 5**

samf-junior-2011-r2-20.title: Each digit equally often
samf-junior-2011-r2-20.body:
There are $5\cdot4\cdot3=60$ such numbers. In each position, each of $1,3,5,7,9$ appears equally often, namely $\frac{60}{5}=12$ times, so the digits in each column add to $12\cdot25=300$. The total is $300\cdot100+300\cdot10+300=33\,300$.

**Answer: (B) 33 300**
